items.summary: The laws of physics are CPT-symmetric, yet laboratory quantum mechanics prepares the past and only samples the future. This working paper distinguishes five levels of taking the symmetry seriously — symmetric laws with the open future left implicit, a two-boundary description, symmetric processes, a nontrivial final boundary, and laboratory access to it — places published views and experiments on them, and states what each predicts for a final-boundary test, in which an engineered terminal acts on a flag and an entangled partner is read on every trial. Exact results: an open future propagates backward through any physical channel; a terminal can only transfer, never manufacture, final-side contrast, giving lambda = tanh(hbar omega / 2 k T_f) in a swap model, the mirror of a reset; a clamp of budget A needs an energy of at least k T_f ln A in some branch; under free local control any every-trial final condition signals, with visibility equal to the clamp strength. Under stated transfer models a null reads as a lower bound on a swap-equivalent final temperature (Partridge: above 3.5e7 K for escaping microwaves; planned qubit tests: about 27 K and 360 K). The paper audits transport to the future, specifies what any physical source of a final condition must supply, and finds that no named candidate meets the specification. CPT motivates the reversed-resource question; channel duality bounds its possible transfer; laboratory access remains an additional physical hypothesis, decided only by experiment. No new experimental result is reported. Drafted with AI assistance and revised after AI-assisted reviews; responsibility rests with the author.

items.summary: Berggren's three matrices generate the tree of primitive Pythagorean triples and preserve the quadratic form x₁² + x₂² − x₃². Cha, Nguyen and Tauber (2018) built such trees for other integral ternary forms Q of signature (2,1). We ask whether the matrices alone determine Q. Main results: Recovery criterion (Theorem 3.1). A set of isometries of Q determines Q up to scale exactly when no nonzero vector is sent to plus or minus itself by all of them. Equivalently, the group they generate is not virtually abelian; for integral isometries, it acts irreducibly. The proof is elementary linear algebra and applies to arbitrary real groups. Berggren trees (Theorem 3.2, Proposition 3.3, Remark 3.5). Any two generators determine Q in Berggren's tree and in each of the five trees of Cha, Nguyen and Tauber. The definition of a Berggren tree alone does not force this: the generators A and A² give a Berggren forest for x₁² + x₂² − x₃² whose two generators both yield edges but do not determine Q. Roots at a rational null line (Theorem 3.6). For a primitive null vector P with divisor G, the minimum of Q on (P^⊥ ∩ ℤ³) \ ℤP is S = |det(2J)|/(2G²). An explicit congruence, Gm ≡ −τ (mod S), decides which minimal vectors e + mP are roots. N-cusps (Theorems 3.7–3.8, Corollary 3.9). For Q = ax₁² + bx₁x₂ + cx₂² − Nx₃² with D = b² − 4ac < 0, all data at the null vectors (p, q, 1) are explicit. A minimal root exists there if and only if gcd(G, S) divides D/G, and in particular whenever D is cube-free. Recovery by integral reflections (Theorem 3.12, Proposition 3.13). Minimal roots at two or three distinct rational null lines yield three integral reflections that determine Q. The paper also relates the reflections in the trees of Cha, Nguyen and Tauber to minimal roots (Remark 3.17), and states an open question for trees produced by their construction.
items.title: The Inverse Berggren Tree Problem

items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly construct multi-agent workflows that decompose a complex task and assign specialist agents from a pool. However, building such a workflow well remains challenging: how finely to divide the task, which agent to trust with each subtask, and when to create a new specialist are all critical decisions a workflow constructor needs to settle up front. Thus, whether each subtask succeeds remains unknown until the workflow runs. Yet, improving a workflow is costly. Locating a fault usually requires a reference answer, a graded outcome, or a trained assessor, and the fix is applied to the whole workflow through re-execution, re-search, or retraining. We propose InFlowOp, which prices every decision in one label-free cost that weighs how well an agent's competence meets what a subtask demands against how much that agent takes to run. Before execution, InFlowOp bidirectionally determines the granularity of task decomposition and agent assignment following from the cost rather than from a fixed template. During execution, InFlowOp corrects a fault with the cheapest move via the same cost that serves the workflow both as it is built and as it runs. Facing the workflow-level evaluation challenge, we introduce Braid, a benchmark whose tasks require multi-agent coordination beyond single-agent capability. Across various domains and backbones, InFlowOp outperforms single agent baselines by up to $+11.97\%$, achieving $+9.64\%$ with in-flow optimization. Our project page: https://xhguo7.github.io/InFlowOp/.
items.title: Pay for the Fault, Not the Flow: Label-Free In-Flow Multi-Agent Workflow Optimization

This plugin is being developed as part of the Physical Sciences Data Infrastructure programme to improve the practices around data within the Physical Sciences remit area within the UK.
items.title: aiida-amber

items.summary: This dataset was produced using a harmonised methodology for estimating the spatial distribution of citrus areas across the European Union at 10 × 10 km grid resolution for the 2020 reference year. The approach integrates Eurostat **Farm Structure Survey (FSS) 2020** gridded agricultural statistics, official regional agricultural statistics and the Copernicus High Resolution Layer (HRL) Crop Types. Missing or suppressed FSS values are estimated using regional crop-area totals and Earth Observation-derived spatial weights, while reported values are transferred, aggregated or disaggregated to the common EEA reference grid according to their source resolution. The resulting map provides quantitative citrus-area estimates, crop-presence indicators, provenance metadata and a rule-based methodological uncertainty class for each grid cell. Evaluation against official regional statistics and independent **Land Use/Cover Area Frame Survey (LUCAS)** field observations showed overall consistency with the source statistics and a 95.1% detection rate for LUCAS-positive grid cells. The resulting spatial dataset is intended to support EFSA plant health risk assessment and related spatial analyses.
items.title: Spatial distribution of citrus areas in the European Union at 10 × 10 km grid resolution, 2020

items.summary: This repository provides the reproducibility package accompanying the manuscript “Cross-fire transferability of four-year NBR-based spectral recovery after the 2021 wildfires in southwestern Türkiye”. The package contains the analysis-ready modelling sample, Google Earth Engine and Python analysis scripts, locked out-of-fold model predictions, model-selection records, sensitivity-analysis outputs, uncertainty and calibration results, derived tables and figures, random seeds, data dictionaries, provenance information, and supporting quality-control documentation. The study evaluates the transferability of four-year NBR-based spectral recovery across five 2021 wildfire complexes in southwestern Türkiye using outer leave-one-fire-out validation and spatially blocked inner cross-validation. The repository supports reproduction and auditing of the reported analyses. Source Sentinel-2, CORINE Land Cover, EFFIS, MODIS MCD64A1, and other third-party datasets remain subject to their original providers’ terms and licences. Spectral recovery reported in this study should not be interpreted as complete biomass, ecosystem, or restoration recovery.
items.title: Reproducibility package for cross-fire transferability of four-year NBR-based spectral recovery after the 2021 wildfires in southwestern Türkiye

items.summary: The Olist Transactional Evidence Benchmark (OTEB) is a neutral, derived research dataset for evaluating analytical methods under incomplete, conflicting, ambiguous, and reconstructable transactional evidence. OTEB is derived from the Brazilian E-Commerce Public Dataset by Olist . It provides a frozen reference cohort of 94,791 internally reconciled orders, 901 deterministic controlled instances, transaction-instance membership, evaluator-only oracle states, and state-specific monetary exposure. The benchmark represents four evidence states: `CONFIRMED`, `RECONSTRUCTED`, `CONFLICTING`, and `UNRESOLVED`. Controlled families cover missing evidence, hard conflicts, unique reconstruction, ambiguous reconstruction, duplicate evidence, and mixed corruption at 5%, 10%, 20%, 30%, and 40%. This release contains the reference oracle, controlled-instance definitions, compact membership index, exposure tables, data dictionary, provenance documentation, reconstruction code, validation code, manifests, schema catalog, and checksums. It contains no method predictions, comparative performance results, ablation studies, paper drafts, dashboards, or private Rahaskin data. Raw Olist CSV files are not redistributed and must be obtained from the original Kaggle source. Original source citation: Olist, & Sionek, A. (2018). items.summary: Code, partition manifests and per-image predictions supporting the audit and leakage-controlled re-evaluation of the 4,217-image Eye Disease Retinal Images collection.   Contents: the provenance and integrity audit; the manifests defining every evaluation arm image by image (image-level, patient-grouped, size-matched, source-matched, the common test set and the six leave-one-source-out splits); the training and evaluation code; stored per-image class probabilities for every run; the shortcut probes; and the visual adjudication verdicts for all 335 cross-label near-duplicate candidates.   The image collection itself is not redistributed here. items.summary: This archive accompanies “Provenance-Aware Quality Control for Heterogeneous Bioactivity Data” by Xin Gao. It contains cached benchmark and fresh-target prediction tables, finite-pair curation summaries, cross-repository comparison materials, figure source tables, frozen manifests, and reproduction code for the non-hosted analyses. Run `python3 tools/recalculate_public_limited_companion.py` after extraction. The standard-library checker reconstructs retained confusion counts, Matthews correlation coefficients, pairwise disagreement summaries, and repository disagreement tiers without network access. This is a cached-statistics reproduction, not an end-to-end replay of every raw data pipeline or a hosted-model rerun. This is a conservative packaging decision and does not claim that the excluded material is necessarily restricted. Software is MIT-licensed; ChEMBL-derived adaptations retain applicable CC BY-SA obligations. BindingDB source dumps and publisher PDFs are not included.

items.summary: Recent video-based world models pair the scalability of autoregressive (AR) prediction with the visual quality of diffusion models. The choice of scene tokenizer is paramount for the optimal performance of each of these, both in terms of fidelity and semantics. Flexible-length, coarse-to-fine tokenizers yield exactly that: the first coarse tokens carry the clip's global semantics while later tokens further specify details. Existing flexible tokenizers only apply a representation-alignment (REPA) loss on early decoder hidden states, a target the decoder can partly meet from its noised input instead. We introduce SemanTok, a flexible video tokenizer that feeds frozen DINO features into its encoder and adds lightweight heads that reconstruct them from each retained token prefix alone. SemanTok achieves high semantic alignment and video fidelity at every AR model size: a 201M SemanTok AR model matches or beats a VideoFlexTok AR model $3.4\times$ its size, and larger SemanTok AR models further improve fidelity. It keeps semantic alignment on out-of-distribution classes and gives the decoder higher semantic alignment at every noise level, including pure noise. It performs well in both reconstruction and generation, and its short token prefixes are cheaper to predict and give better generation fidelity, with pixel detail deferred to later tokens.
items.title: SemanTok: Predictable Semantic Tokens for Efficient Autoregressive Video Generation

items.summary: Controlling an agent with vision requires being able to separate useful information from irrelevant background information. JEPA-style latent world models seem like a natural approach for this, as they do not perform pixel-level reconstruction; however, they are still sensitive to these distractor signals and experience latent collapse. In this work, we introduce Controllability Factorized JEPA (CF-JEPA), a JEPA-style world model which splits the latent space into controllable and uncontrollable subspaces. This factorization allows us to capture all the distractor information into the uncontrollable region, while we use the control-relevant latent information for our task. With this, we show comparable performance across 2D and 3D control tasks under nominal conditions and improved performance under distracted conditions, where CF-JEPA is the only model that does not experience latent collapse. We also validate our model under distracted conditions for a simulated robot task, highlighting the practical application of such a scheme.
items.title: CF-JEPA: Improving Robustness of JEPA World Models via Controllability Factorization

items.summary: This repository provides the compiled analysis inputs, R code, figure source data and GIS rasters supporting the manuscript “Historical introduction pools pre-structure future plant invasion debt under climate change”. Version 2.0 contains the final USA-intersection climatic-analogue reconstruction and its corresponding model predictions and spatial summaries. The historical introduction pool contains 18,562 species. The stage-transition models use 5,791 complete-case species, of which 4,088 species without a recorded invasion form the future candidate invasion-debt subset. Future predictions cover 12 combinations of two climate scenarios (SSP126 and SSP585), three periods (2041–2060, 2061–2080 and 2081–2100), and two global climate models (HadGEM3-GC31-LL and MPI-ESM1-2-HR). The archive contains: • Figure_data: XLSX source workbooks for main Figures 1–4, Supplementary Figures S1–S4 and Supplementary Tables S1–S15, together with the compiled species-level analysis dataset and current and future candidate-species predictions. • Code: R scripts, computational inputs and provenance documentation for the stage-transition models, climatic-analogue searches, future predictions, phylogenetic null analysis, temporal analyses, sensitivity analyses and publication source tables. • GIS_rasters: GeoTIFFs for the main and supplementary spatial figures. Main Figure 4 rasters contain sums within globally aligned 0.5° display cells; supplementary spatial rasters retain the native 10-arc-minute resolution. • Validation: execution records and numerical checks. • README files: instructions for reproducing the analyses, plotting the source data and interpreting the spatial fields. Current and future closest US climatic analogue cells are identified separately for each candidate species. POT is the sum of future predicted invasion probabilities assigned to future analogue cells. CHG is future grid-level transition potential minus current grid-level transition potential, with unassigned cells completed with zero. CHG therefore incorporates both changes in predicted probability and relocation of climatic analogues. POSDP is the sum of positive species-level changes assigned to future analogue cells; Supplementary Figure S3 reports its range across the two climate models. The analytical workflow was tested with R 4.3.3. Reproduction starts from the compiled historical master dataset, supplied phylogenetic inputs, prepared species climatic centroids and extracted WorldClim grid values. The package does not independently repeat every upstream archive-curation decision, manual stage-status assignment, GBIF download or occurrence-cleaning step. These boundaries and the optional XLSX and GeoTIFF export procedures are documented in the README. The historical count of 15,950 candidate invasion-debt species is retained for historical summaries; it is not the population used for future predictions. This release supersedes the earlier spatial outputs based on a rectangular climate-search domain. Future results should be interpreted as conditional model projections rather than evidence of a statistically established climate-driven increase in invasion. The repository record is distributed under CC BY 4.0. The software license included in Code/LICENSE and the original terms of third-party inputs remain applicable.
items.title: Data and code for "Historical introduction pools pre-structure future plant invasion debt under climate change"

items.summary: World models allow agents to plan in latent space by choosing a sequence of actions that most reduces the distance to a given goal state. Thus, planning can benefit from latent representations whose distances mirror commute-times in the environment. The spectral embedding space of the graph Laplacian provides such a representation, if it obeys a specific eigenvalue-dependent scaling. Unfortunately, instantiating the graph Laplacian is intractable in large, continuous environments. Self-supervised learning offers a natural route to such commute-time-preserving embeddings at scale. However, here we show that existing methods, which commonly encourage isotropic representations to prevent representational collapse, tend to degrade the "correct" eigenvalue-dependent scaling, leading to an inaccurate representation of commute times. To address this problem, we introduce Commute-Time-Preserving World Models (CTWMs), combining a latent displacement predictor and a log-determinant regularizer that prevents collapse, which provably recover the correctly scaled Laplacian representation under reversible deterministic dynamics and at the predictor's fixed point. In numerical simulations, CTWM matches or outperforms LeWM, a task-agnostic baseline, on several complex, continuous goal-reaching benchmarks, while using half the parameters.
items.title: Learning Commute-Time-Preserving World Models for Planning

items.summary: This software archive contains the complete CEG0–CEG6 Lean 4 formal-verification chain developed to connect the Chronos entropy Arrow construction with a generalized finite relative-entropy functional, a finite spectral entropy/gravity kernel, matrix traces, similarity-invariant operator representations, and the canonical spectral decomposition of arbitrary finite positive-definite real matrices. The chain begins with the generalized relative entropy Lean verifies that equal-mass inputs reduce this functional to finite Kullback–Leibler divergence. The previously verified Chronos EN1–EN6 complete-coarse-graining Arrow increment and rate are then connected directly to this D_+ functional. An explicit calibration interface links the entropy Arrow to the older Chronos Change/Arrow/Action clock system without assuming that the two independently defined Arrow quantities are identical. The bridge is subsequently lifted from scalar expressions to diagonal matrices and traces. in the diagonal spectral representation. Similarity invariance is then formally established, removing dependence on the chosen basis. The final CEG6 stage instantiates the construction using Mathlib's finite Hermitian spectral theorem for an arbitrary positive-definite real matrix G. The canonical eigenvector unitary, its two-sided inverse, strictly positive eigenvalues, the operator-trace identity, and the scaled finite spectral Lambda relation are all kernel checked. All final stages, CEG0 v0.5, CEG1 v0.3, CEG2 v0.3, CEG3 v0.2, CEG4 v0.2, CEG5 v0.2, and CEG6 v0.1, passed static placeholder audits and Lean axiom audits. The audited theorem dependencies report only propext , Classical.choice , and Quot.sound , with no sorryAx . The archive establishes a finite-dimensional mathematical compatibility chain. It does not assume that a Chronos physical state and an external geometric G-field are physically identical; where such a cross-framework state identification is required, the compatibility condition remains explicit in the formalization. Description This updated release extends the Lean-Verified Chronos Entropy–Gravity Bridge from CEG0–CEG6 through the new CEG7 field-to-measurement stage. The cumulative formal program connects the Chronos temporal framework to entropy production, generalized relative entropy, matrix and operator structure, positive-definite spectral geometry, gravity, and now an explicit experimentally testable prediction. The earlier CEG0–CEG6 stages formally established a chain from the Chronos entropy Arrow through generalized relative entropy into a finite positive-definite operator representation. The later stages removed dependence on a chosen basis and used Mathlib’s spectral theorem to connect the construction to arbitrary finite positive-definite real matrices. CEG7 adds the next important step. It connects the previously verified Chronos radial time field and its Newtonian gravity correspondence to a proposed gradient-dependent effective gravitational coupling. This produces a concrete predicted environmental shift in the measured gravitational coupling rather than only reproducing the standard Newtonian limit. The package also includes a formally verified comparison with a constant-coupling baseline. Lean proves that the constant baseline produces no environmental shift, while the Chronos model can produce a nonzero field-dependent shift. An explicit measurement-resolution theorem is included, showing the conditions under which an experiment would be able to distinguish the Chronos prediction from the zero-shift baseline. The cumulative CEG0–CEG7 chain therefore connects: Chronos temporal field → gravity → entropy → information structure → positive-definite operator geometry → measurable gravitational prediction. All final stages included in this release passed Lean verification in the pinned environment. Static source audits found no sorry , admit , o
items.title: Lean-Verified Chronos Entropy–Gravity Bridge: From Entropy Production to Positive-Definite Spectral Operators — CEG0–CEG6-CEG7

items.summary: World Action Models (WAMs) predict visual futures and robot actions, yet they remain susceptible to task-incomplete imagination, where plausible, action-consistent predictions omit the transition needed for task completion. In this paper, we show that this failure is not inherent to the world model backbone, but emerges when adapted for short-chunk control, which can repeatedly favor plausible local continuations over task-completing transitions. To address this, we introduce Completion Aware Guidance (CAG), a training-free sampling method that guides generation toward task completion. Across representative WAMs, CAG improves success from 64% to 70% on a RoboTwin 2.0 subset and from 69% to 75% in zero-shot simulation, while reducing task-incomplete imagination from 79% to 40%.
items.title: Completion Aware Guidance for World Action Models

items.summary: ARC-AGI-3 evaluates agents in interactive environments whose rules and objectives must be inferred from observation. We present Kepler, an open-source harness that represents hypotheses as executable world models and validates them through retrospective transition checks and conditional prediction checks. Under one frozen Claude Opus 5 configuration, Kepler obtained a server-verified 100.00 RHAE on all 25 public games, with no per-game model selection or score-conditioned reruns. On 181 of 183 completed levels, the final Opus attempt used no more actions than the corresponding median-human baseline. The retained board runs used 8,256 environment actions, of which 7,292 occurred in scored levels. Retained local provider-session records yield 858.0 million tokens, 97.37% cache reads, and a \$777.72 cost at September 1, 2026 API list-equivalent rates. We also report three evaluation failures: source-code leakage that produced an invalid perfect run, agents reconstructing a removed harness in a control condition, and autonomous repair masking a broken planner. A single-game observation case study showed that animation frames contained task-relevant information absent from settled text grids. Across the final Claude Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol boards, 48 of 50 game-model cells reached 100. These results indicate that public-set score alone has limited discriminative value and motivate first-attempt, cost-conditioned, and verification-aware reporting.
items.title: Kepler: Auditable World Models for ARC-AGI-3

items.summary: End-to-end research agents can now produce complete scientific papers, yet manuscript claims often diverge from executed experiments. This gap is structural: research state, failure histories, and claim-evidence alignment are not maintained as persistent, verifiable state across long-horizon pipelines. We present YouRA (Your Research Agent), an architecture for stateful, evidence-traceable autonomous research. YouRA preserves research state, execution evidence, and failure history across the research trajectory by integrating three components: a Verification State Architecture (VSA) that tracks hypotheses, gates, and evidence pointers; an Independent Controller that turns state and reflection records into lifecycle, recovery, and debate/review control while separating control from execution; and Stateful Reflection that logs failures as structured lessons and routes recovery through bounded repair, redesign, or reset. On MLR-Bench's predefined ten-task end-to-end subset, YouRA improves over both MLR-Agent and AI Scientist V2 on scalar Overall across all three matched backbones. An automated diagnostic using MLR-Bench's hallucination taxonomy reports intersection/union counts for four fact-based failure types, and data-provenance diagnostic shows more real-data-based outputs. Ablating each of the four components (the VSA, the Independent Controller, MCP tool access, and reflection-guided recovery) supports their separable contributions. Removing either core-state component drops YouRA below the full system. Code: https://github.com/PrayPrey/Your-Research-Agent.
items.title: YouRA: A Persistent-State Architecture for Evidence-Traceable Autonomous Research Agents

items.summary: Privacy-derived scientific materials for controlled studies of evidence access and adverse product content in AI assessment. The supplement contains synthetic materials, prompts, recorded model answers, terminal failures, assignment mappings, original stage-specific scoring and statistical implementations, reference results, and an offline CPU replay entrypoint. It includes the main local studies, the hosted-model study, historical screening, two common-interface qualification rounds, and the exploratory two-model pilot. Screening and development records are kept distinct from formal comparisons; reused answer aliases are not independent generations. The qualification amendment was made after qualification and before the exploratory pilot, and the subsequent proposed formal extension was not run. The findings do not establish a general advantage of pre-event defense, equivalence, or broad robustness. This is a redacted scientific derivative with a new integrity manifest: account authorizations, user dialogue, machine paths, hardware logs, original provider envelopes, encrypted reasoning, native token journals and model weights are excluded. CPU replay reproduces scores and statistics from the released scientific records; it does not regenerate answers or repeat the original private token/authorization/environment audits.
items.title: Scientific supplement for Evidence Access and Adverse Product Content in AI Assessment

items.summary: A persistent agent must decide both what to retain as information arrives and what to surface once a query appears, yet memory evaluations can confound these decisions by comparing methods that differ in both retention and selection. We build a streaming-recall benchmark crossing retention and selection rules and evaluate every condition on the same 300 seeded episodes. Holding access fixed, query-aware selection improves required-fact recall by 15.5 percentage points (95% CI: 12.8 to 18.2), whereas a mixed comparison that also changes history access reports a 68.7-point advantage, of which 53.2 points are attributable to access. Under bounded retention, query-aware, dense, and oracle selection reach the retention ceiling, and all 319 observed failures in the bounded recency condition are caused by eviction rather than ranking errors. Recall falls to 0% as targets recede sufficiently far into the past. Repeating the evaluation on SQuAD preserves the retention ceiling while showing that dense retrieval can outperform lexical retrieval on natural text. These results show that bounded-memory evaluations should hold access fixed and report retention and selection separately.
items.title: What Should an Agent Remember? Disentangling Retention from Retrieval in Bounded-Memory Evaluation

items.summary: Recent video-based world models pair the scalability of autoregressive (AR) prediction with the visual quality of diffusion models. The choice of scene tokenizer is paramount for the optimal performance of each of these, both in terms of fidelity and semantics. Flexible-length, coarse-to-fine tokenizers yield exactly that: the first coarse tokens carry the clip's global semantics while later tokens further specify details. Existing flexible tokenizers only apply a representation-alignment (REPA) loss on early decoder hidden states, a target the decoder can partly meet from its noised input instead. We introduce SemanTok, a flexible video tokenizer that feeds frozen DINO features into its encoder and adds lightweight heads that reconstruct them from each retained token prefix alone. SemanTok achieves high semantic alignment and video fidelity at every AR model size: a 201M SemanTok AR model matches or beats a VideoFlexTok AR model $3.4\times$ its size, and larger SemanTok AR models further improve fidelity. It keeps semantic alignment on out-of-distribution classes and gives the decoder higher semantic alignment at every noise level, including pure noise. It performs well in both reconstruction and generation, and its short token prefixes are cheaper to predict and give better generation fidelity, with pixel detail deferred to later tokens.
items.title: SemanTok: Predictable Semantic Tokens for Efficient Autoregressive Video Generation

items.summary: World models allow agents to plan in latent space by choosing a sequence of actions that most reduces the distance to a given goal state. Thus, planning can benefit from latent representations whose distances mirror commute-times in the environment. The spectral embedding space of the graph Laplacian provides such a representation, if it obeys a specific eigenvalue-dependent scaling. Unfortunately, instantiating the graph Laplacian is intractable in large, continuous environments. Self-supervised learning offers a natural route to such commute-time-preserving embeddings at scale. However, here we show that existing methods, which commonly encourage isotropic representations to prevent representational collapse, tend to degrade the "correct" eigenvalue-dependent scaling, leading to an inaccurate representation of commute times. To address this problem, we introduce Commute-Time-Preserving World Models (CTWMs), combining a latent displacement predictor and a log-determinant regularizer that prevents collapse, which provably recover the correctly scaled Laplacian representation under reversible deterministic dynamics and at the predictor's fixed point. In numerical simulations, CTWM matches or outperforms LeWM, a task-agnostic baseline, on several complex, continuous goal-reaching benchmarks, while using half the parameters.
items.title: Learning Commute-Time-Preserving World Models for Planning

items.summary: Video temporal grounding aims to localize events in videos from natural-language queries. For agents built around frozen video-language models, the harness determines how queries guide temporal predictions and how those predictions are refined. Manually refining these harnesses requires diagnosing grounding failures and coordinating changes to both agent workflows and instructions. We introduce VideoEvolve, a framework that automatically evolves agent harnesses for video temporal grounding. VideoEvolve uses a Cloze-Structured Harness Representation that preserves stage interfaces while leaving agent workflows and instructions open to evolution. Branch-Guided Harness Evolution preserves promising code branches for continued refinement, using execution feedback to guide local edits and validation to determine which improvements are carried forward. Experiments demonstrate improved grounding performance across multiple benchmarks. Component analyses identify instruction refinement as a consistent source of gains, while the benefits of evolved code vary across evaluation settings. Together, these results support automated harness evolution as an effective approach to improving video temporal grounding. Code is available at https://github.com/bingjunluo/VideoEvolve .
items.title: VideoEvolve: Evolving Agent Harnesses for Video Temporal Grounding

items.summary: Cooperative MARL is commonly evaluated through cooperation discovery from random initialization, leaving open whether continued optimization can destabilize learned cooperation. Actor-critic comparisons can also conflate critic presence with value gradients entering shared actor representations. We study cooperation maintenance, defined as the survival of a behaviorally verified cooperative policy under continued training. We formulate maintenance as a right-censored event-time problem and compare matched warm starts: X0 allows value loss gradients to update shared actor features, X1 retains the critic while blocking those gradients, and X5 removes the learned critic as a critic-free reference. This isolates direct value-gradient access while controlling initialization, critic computation, and evaluation. Positive reward scaling preserves strategic preferences and equilibria while perturbing learning dynamics. Gradient audits confirm the intended routing pathways, and frozen-policy torso perturbations probe whether route-induced updates align with local cooperation boundaries. In confirmatory MinEx and CleanUp-lite experiments, higher scales selectively increase maintenance sensitivity in X0; X1 remains near the censoring ceiling, and X5 has no confirmed events in the tested settings. In CleanUp-lite, route-by-scale displacement is associated with reduced local cooperation margins; MinEx shows a weaker, optimizer-dependent effect. These results identify a conditional, scale-sensitive maintenance risk associated with direct value-gradient routing rather than a universal failure of critics.
items.title: After Cooperation Is Learned: Gradient Routing and Optimizer-Dependent Maintenance in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

items.summary: Documentation-only release. Numerical implementation, compression tolerances and defaults are unchanged from v0.1.2. The website now explains what led to the accuracy, memory and throughput advances: Inherited interaction directions, partner QR weighting and empty parent bases. Stored adjoints and consistent energy derivatives; strict rank-cap checks and transactional recompression. Reusable scratch, implicit saturated bases, contiguous packet products and safe concurrent reductions. Real PLAG066 mesh provenance, common-input LEM/NEB protocol, physical error gates, measured results and limitations. The separate 244 MB relaxed-tolerance experiment and the selected tight-tolerance 303 MB result. Added an explanatory diagram, downloadable CSV evidence with SHA-256 ledger, and a self-contained rectangular reference example. Updated the practical configuration guide, corrected the nested-basis formula and qualified rank-dependent scaling claims. The local Documenter build passes, all 248 checked local links/anchors and evidence hashes pass, and the new example passes on Julia 1.13.1. Julia 1.13 or later remains required. Read the updated algorithm explanation , practical guide , and validation evidence .
items.title: duserzym/H2Matrices.jl: H2Matrices.jl v0.1.3 — documentation update

items.summary: This record contains the replication package accompanying the article “DCMT-Cert: Empirical Adequacy Certification of Machine-Learning Data-Contract Gates.” The package provides the scripts, retained numerical outputs, analysis tables, audit materials, dataset manifests, source hashes, and checksum information required to reproduce and inspect the computational analyses reported in the article. The materials cover the paired clean-versus-clean harm calibration, the Stage 1 policy-development analysis, the Stage 2 confirmation analysis, all five prespecified operating profiles, policy selection and multiplicity analyses, baseline comparisons, broadened fault analyses, model-family validation, native Great Expectations validation, harm-threshold sensitivity, provenance and transfer audits, and supporting consistency checks. The package is organised using descriptive file names and is intended to permit independent inspection and reproduction of the reported computational results. The accompanying article defines the experimental protocol, scope of the empirical certificates, statistical interpretation, and limitations of the study.
items.title: Replication Package for "DCMT-Cert: Empirical Adequacy Certification of Machine-Learning Data-Contract Gates"

items.summary: Civil Engineering Explained: Infrastructure, Systems & Built Environment Design is an open educational resource (OER) curriculum module establishing the core engineering principles, mathematical formulations, and contemporary computational paradigms underpinning the modern built environment. The module establishes a rigorous systems engineering foundation spanning seven major sub-disciplines: Structural Engineering: Limit state design, load paths, second-order effects, ductility requirements, and advanced materials (UHPC, CFRP). Geotechnical Engineering: Soil mechanics, effective stress balance, Darcy's law, and deep/shallow foundation systems. Transportation Engineering: Macroscopic traffic flow dynamics, signal timing splits, and demand management. Water Resources Engineering: Rational method hydrology, rainfall-runoff modeling, and sustainable urban drainage systems (SuDS). Urban and Regional Planning: Transit-oriented development, microclimate adaptation, and spatial systems trade-offs. Construction Management: BIM Level 2/3 coordination, CPM/PERT scheduling, and lifecycle asset tracking. Earthquake and Disaster Engineering: Seismic base isolation, elastoplastic dynamic response, and community resilience. Key Pedagogical Features: AI-Era Computational Bridges: Integration of Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), Fourier Neural Operators (FNOs), and Kalman-filtered (IEKF/UKF) edge digital twins for real-time structural health monitoring. Systems Engineering Trade-Off Matrix: Multi-variable evaluation across structural, seismic, geotechnical, and drainage domains balancing lifecycle carbon, capital cost, and failure modes. Worked Numerical Application: Step-by-step limit state design calculation for a singly reinforced concrete beam in flexure, verifying ductility and moment capacity per ACI 318 / Eurocode 2. Interactive Tool: Algorithmic formulation of the Rational Method peak runoff and hydrograph curve dynamics. Comprehensive Assessment: Curated foundational, scenario-based, and multi-step numerical engineering problem sets.
items.title: Civil Engineering Explained: Infrastructure, Systems & Built Environment Design

items.summary: The Olist Transactional Evidence Benchmark (OTEB) is a neutral, derived research dataset for evaluating analytical methods under incomplete, conflicting, ambiguous, and reconstructable transactional evidence. OTEB is derived from the Brazilian E-Commerce Public Dataset by Olist . It provides a frozen reference cohort of 94,791 internally reconciled orders, 901 deterministic controlled instances, transaction-instance membership, evaluator-only oracle states, and state-specific monetary exposure. The benchmark represents four evidence states: `CONFIRMED`, `RECONSTRUCTED`, `CONFLICTING`, and `UNRESOLVED`. Controlled families cover missing evidence, hard conflicts, unique reconstruction, ambiguous reconstruction, duplicate evidence, and mixed corruption at 5%, 10%, 20%, 30%, and 40%. This release contains the reference oracle, controlled-instance definitions, compact membership index, exposure tables, data dictionary, provenance documentation, reconstruction code, validation code, manifests, schema catalog, and checksums. It contains no method predictions, comparative performance results, ablation studies, paper drafts, dashboards, or private Rahaskin data. Raw Olist CSV files are not redistributed and must be obtained from the original Kaggle source. Original source citation: Olist, & Sionek, A. (2018). Brazilian E-Commerce Public Dataset by Olist [Data set]. Kaggle. https://doi.org/10.34740/KAGGLE/DSV/195341 Official source: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/olistbr/brazilian-ecommerce License: Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 International (`CC BY-NC-SA 4.0`).
items.title: Olist Transactional Evidence Benchmark (OTEB)

items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly construct multi-agent workflows that decompose a complex task and assign specialist agents from a pool. However, building such a workflow well remains challenging: how finely to divide the task, which agent to trust with each subtask, and when to create a new specialist are all critical decisions a workflow constructor needs to settle up front. Thus, whether each subtask succeeds remains unknown until the workflow runs. Yet, improving a workflow is costly. Locating a fault usually requires a reference answer, a graded outcome, or a trained assessor, and the fix is applied to the whole workflow through re-execution, re-search, or retraining. We propose InFlowOp, which prices every decision in one label-free cost that weighs how well an agent's competence meets what a subtask demands against how much that agent takes to run. Before execution, InFlowOp bidirectionally determines the granularity of task decomposition and agent assignment following from the cost rather than from a fixed template. During execution, InFlowOp corrects a fault with the cheapest move via the same cost that serves the workflow both as it is built and as it runs. Facing the workflow-level evaluation challenge, we introduce Braid, a benchmark whose tasks require multi-agent coordination beyond single-agent capability. Across various domains and backbones, InFlowOp outperforms single agent baselines by up to $+11.97\%$, achieving $+9.64\%$ with in-flow optimization. Our project page: https://xhguo7.github.io/InFlowOp/.
items.title: Pay for the Fault, Not the Flow: Label-Free In-Flow Multi-Agent Workflow Optimization

items.summary: A time series world model (TSWM) predicts a controlled system's state from its observed history and planned actions and exogenous inputs. Current approaches build forecasters with actions as covariates, trained and evaluated on prediction error under the executed plan. Yet world models compare unexecuted plans, but their responses to changed plans remain untested. We ask which design choices matter and whether accurate forecasters respond to changed plans as real systems do. We address both with a formalization and benchmark. The formalization separates state, actions and exogenous inputs, distinguishes continuous, mode and event actions, and introduces mechanism consistency, a metric built on declared action-state relations with known directions, such as a vasopressor raising blood pressure: it checks whether shifting an action moves the forecast in the declared direction. The benchmark consolidates eight public datasets with real actions from engineered infrastructure and clinical care, varying prediction space, plan fusion and plan encoding across seven backbones and five seeds. First, a frozen latent prediction space lowers MAE by 9.9% over observation space and gated output fusion lowers it by 12.7% over input concatenation on average, with both improving all eight datasets; temporal plan encoding changes average MAE by at most 2.2%. Second, prediction error and mechanism consistency diverge: the lowest-error configuration is at or below chance in consistency on four of five datasets with declared mechanisms, and no design choice avoids this. Finally, directional supervision, a loss penalizing the wrong-signed part of the response to a shifted action, significantly raises consistency on penalized mechanisms with no change in MAE. Together they give TSWMs a recipe: a frozen latent space and output-side fusion for accuracy, and a training objective for mechanism consistency.
items.title: On the Divergence of Accuracy and Mechanism Consistency in Time Series World Models

items.summary: This archive accompanies “Provenance-Aware Quality Control for Heterogeneous Bioactivity Data” by Xin Gao. It contains cached benchmark and fresh-target prediction tables, finite-pair curation summaries, cross-repository comparison materials, figure source tables, frozen manifests, and reproduction code for the non-hosted analyses. Run `python3 tools/recalculate_public_limited_companion.py` after extraction. The standard-library checker reconstructs retained confusion counts, Matthews correlation coefficients, pairwise disagreement summaries, and repository disagreement tiers without network access. This is a cached-statistics reproduction, not an end-to-end replay of every raw data pipeline or a hosted-model rerun. The archive deliberately excludes hosted-model MAPK14 per-item and aggregate outputs, Figure 8 source material, and raw payload, CIF, and run files because accepted-account redistribution terms were not retrieved. This is a conservative packaging decision and does not claim that the excluded material is necessarily restricted. Software is MIT-licensed; ChEMBL-derived adaptations retain applicable CC BY-SA obligations. BindingDB source dumps and publisher PDFs are not included.
items.title: Public-limited companion materials for Provenance-Aware Quality Control for Heterogeneous Bioactivity Data

items.summary: Code, partition manifests and per-image predictions supporting the audit and leakage-controlled re-evaluation of the 4,217-image Eye Disease Retinal Images collection.   Contents: the provenance and integrity audit; the manifests defining every evaluation arm image by image (image-level, patient-grouped, size-matched, source-matched, the common test set and the six leave-one-source-out splits); the training and evaluation code; stored per-image class probabilities for every run; the shortcut probes; and the visual adjudication verdicts for all 335 cross-label near-duplicate candidates.   The image collection itself is not redistributed here. It is available at https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/python16/eye-disease-retinal-images and the manifests reference it by relative path.
items.title: Acquisition source confounds a widely used retinal fundus benchmark: audit, partitions and per-run predictions

items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on persistent external sources to solve sequences of knowledge-intensive tasks. Existing methods improve how source content is accessed and organized, while agent-memory systems preserve reusable knowledge from prior interactions, but repeated use of the same source is still largely treated as repeated access rather than an opportunity to progressively improve understanding of that source. We study source learning: developing reusable source-specific competence over a persistent authoritative source. We represent this competence with a persistent source model that captures reusable understanding of the source, including how its knowledge is structured, interpreted, and applied. To construct and progressively refine such models, we propose SourceLearn, which combines two complementary learning mechanisms. Self-Directed Source Learning identifies what remains incompletely understood and adaptively revisits the source, while Task-Guided Source Learning uses downstream experience to reveal local representational gaps and recurring needs in how source knowledge should be organized. In both cases, learning signals determine what should be reconsidered, while persistent updates are reconstructed from the authoritative source. Across five benchmarks and three LLM backends, SourceLearn achieves the best performance in 13 of 15 settings, with gains of up to 22.6 points over Hybrid RAG and substantial overall improvements over static source representations and experience-based memory baselines.
items.title: From Knowledge Access to Source Learning: Developing Source-Specific Competence

items.summary: This repository provides the reproducibility package accompanying the manuscript “Cross-fire transferability of four-year NBR-based spectral recovery after the 2021 wildfires in southwestern Türkiye”. The package contains the analysis-ready modelling sample, Google Earth Engine and Python analysis scripts, locked out-of-fold model predictions, model-selection records, sensitivity-analysis outputs, uncertainty and calibration results, derived tables and figures, random seeds, data dictionaries, provenance information, and supporting quality-control documentation. The study evaluates the transferability of four-year NBR-based spectral recovery across five 2021 wildfire complexes in southwestern Türkiye using outer leave-one-fire-out validation and spatially blocked inner cross-validation. The repository supports reproduction and auditing of the reported analyses. Source Sentinel-2, CORINE Land Cover, EFFIS, MODIS MCD64A1, and other third-party datasets remain subject to their original providers’ terms and licences. Spectral recovery reported in this study should not be interpreted as complete biomass, ecosystem, or restoration recovery.
items.title: Reproducibility package for cross-fire transferability of four-year NBR-based spectral recovery after the 2021 wildfires in southwestern Türkiye
